title: Colorado SB 24-205 AI Chatbot Disclosure: Rulemaking Timeline & Compliance Checklist — Council of AI
context: 2026-09-15 engine cycle — Colorado's SB 24-205 (the Colorado AI Act) was signed May 2024 and is the first US state law to impose comprehensive obligations on high-risk AI systems. Key compliance dates have been phased in throughout 2025-2026. This seed page maps the rulemaking timeline, identifies what is live now (September 2026), and explains how the Council of AI measurement board provides auditable evidence for deployer compliance.
body: Colorado Senate Bill 24-205, the Colorado AI Act, is the first comprehensive US state-level regulation of high-risk artificial intelligence systems. Signed by Governor Polis on May 17, 2024, it establishes obligations for both developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems that make or influence consequential decisions in employment, education, financial services, healthcare, housing, insurance, and legal services. The law's phased implementation timeline is critical for compliance planning. February 1, 2026: The core anti-discrimination provisions and deployer duty-of-care obligations took effect. Deployers of high-risk AI systems must now implement risk management practices, provide notice to consumers when an AI system is a substantial factor in a consequential decision, and offer an opportunity to correct data and appeal adverse outcomes. February 1, 2026 also marks the start of the Attorney General's rulemaking authority to issue implementing regulations, including technical standards for impact assessments and bias audits. The Colorado Attorney General's office published draft rules in Q2 2026 and held public comment through August 2026. Final rules are expected Q4 2026, establishing the specific format and content requirements for algorithmic impact assessments (AIAs). Key open questions in the rulemaking include: what constitutes a 'reasonably sufficient' impact assessment; whether third-party audit credentials (such as the Council of AI's verified measurement credential) will satisfy the AIA requirement; and how the law interacts with existing federal frameworks (EEOC guidance on AI in employment, CFPB guidance on AI in credit). For deployers, the Council of AI measurement board offers a path to compliance evidence. Each of the14 axes measures a specific safety and fairness dimension — bias detection, privacy preservation, care and harm assessment, detector interoperability — across 19+ models with Ed25519-signed manifests. A deployer can point to specific board measurements as evidence of ongoing risk monitoring, satisfying the law's requirement for 'reasonable care' without relying on vendor self-attestation. The verified measurement credential ties each observation to the measuring party and the measurement conditions, which is exactly what an algorithmic impact assessment requires: not just 'we tested it' but 'here is who tested it, when, under what conditions, and what the signed results were.' The Colorado AI Act does not require provable isolation or formal verification of AI behaviour — it requires monitored, documented, ongoing risk management. This is monitored containment in statutory form.
